clues.clue: This command creates a new Git repository in the current directory by generating a hidden .git folder.
clues.explain: git init creates the hidden .git directory that turns a plain folder into a repository, after which Git can track commits and history.

clues.clue: This staging area structure tells Git exactly which changes to include in the next commit snapshot.
clues.response: What is the index (or staging area)?
clues.explain: The staging area (index) is where you assemble exactly which changes go into the next commit, so a commit can be a curated subset of your edits.

clues.clue: This command shows the exact lines added and removed between your working directory and the staging area.
clues.explain: git diff with no args shows unstaged changes (working tree vs index); 'git diff --staged' shows what's staged versus the last commit.

clues.clue: This branching strategy uses short-lived feature branches merged into a single main branch, deleting the branch after merge.
clues.response: What is GitHub Flow (or trunk-based development)?
clues.explain: GitHub Flow / trunk-based development keeps branches short-lived: branch, open a PR, merge to main, delete -- minimizing long divergence and painful merges.

clues.clue: This internal data structure is a directed acyclic graph of commit objects, each pointing to parent commit(s) and a tree object representing the file snapshot.
clues.response: What is the Git commit graph (or Git object model)?
clues.explain: Git's object model is a directed acyclic graph: each commit points to its parent(s) and a tree snapshot, which is how branches, merges, and history traversal work.

clues.clue: This file contains step-by-step instructions to build a Docker image, using directives like FROM, COPY, and RUN.
clues.explain: A Dockerfile is the recipe (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD...) Docker reads to build a reproducible image layer by layer.

clues.clue: This Docker command maps a port on the host machine to a port inside the container, using the -p flag.
clues.response: What is docker run -p (port mapping / publish)?
clues.explain: -p host:container publishes a container port to the host so outside traffic can reach the service (e.g. -p 8080:80).

clues.clue: This technique uses a multi-stage Dockerfile to compile code in one stage and copy only the final binary into a minimal production image.
clues.explain: A multi-stage build compiles in a heavy 'builder' stage, then copies only the final artifact into a tiny runtime image -- smaller and with fewer vulnerabilities.

clues.clue: This Linux kernel feature provides process-level isolation by creating separate namespaces for PID, network, mount points, and more.
clues.explain: Linux namespaces isolate a container's view of PIDs, network, mounts, and users; combined with cgroups (resource limits), they are what make a container.

clues.clue: This filesystem mechanism allows Docker images to share common base layers, storing only the differences in each new layer to save disk space.
clues.response: What is a union filesystem (or overlay filesystem / copy-on-write)?
clues.explain: An overlay/union filesystem stacks read-only image layers under a thin writable layer (copy-on-write), so images share base layers and save disk space.

clues.clue: This is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, consisting of one or more containers that share storage and a network namespace.
clues.explain: A Pod is Kubernetes's smallest unit: one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP) and storage, scheduled together on a node.

clues.clue: This Kubernetes object provides a stable IP address and DNS name, load-balancing traffic across a set of Pods matched by label selectors.
clues.explain: A Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name and load-balances to the Pods matching its label selector, decoupling clients from ephemeral Pod IPs.

clues.clue: This controller ensures a specified number of Pod replicas are running at all times, and manages rolling updates and rollbacks.
clues.explain: A Deployment declares the desired replica count and manages rolling updates and rollbacks via ReplicaSets, keeping that many Pods healthy.

clues.clue: This control plane component watches for newly created Pods with no assigned node and selects the optimal node for them to run on.
clues.explain: The kube-scheduler watches for unscheduled Pods and binds each to the best node based on resources, affinity, taints, and constraints.

clues.clue: This admission controller intercepts API requests before they are persisted, capable of mutating or validating objects. Commonly used for sidecar injection.
clues.response: What is a MutatingAdmissionWebhook (or admission controller)?
clues.explain: An admission webhook intercepts API requests before they're persisted; a mutating one can alter objects (e.g. inject a sidecar) before they're stored.

clues.clue: This practice involves automatically building and testing code every time a developer pushes changes to a shared repository.
clues.explain: Continuous Integration automatically builds and tests every push to the shared repo, catching integration breaks early instead of at one big merge.

clues.clue: This type of pipeline artifact is an immutable, versioned package produced by a build step and consumed by a deployment step.
clues.response: What is a build artifact (or release artifact)?
clues.explain: An artifact is the immutable, versioned output of the build (jar, image, binary) that later stages deploy -- build once, promote the same bits.

clues.clue: This deployment strategy maintains two identical production environments, routing traffic to one while deploying to the other, then switching instantly.
clues.explain: Blue-green keeps two identical production environments; you deploy to the idle one, then flip traffic instantly -- enabling near-zero-downtime cutover and fast rollback.

clues.clue: This practice gradually routes a small percentage of production traffic to a new version, monitoring error rates and latency before full rollout.
clues.response: What is a canary deployment (or canary release)?
clues.explain: A canary release sends a small slice of real traffic to the new version, watching errors and latency before ramping to 100% -- limiting blast radius.

clues.clue: This security practice scans container images in the CI pipeline for known CVEs, blocking deployment if critical vulnerabilities exceed a severity threshold.
clues.response: What is container image scanning (or vulnerability scanning / shift-left security)?
clues.explain: Image scanning checks containers for known CVEs in the pipeline and fails the build over critical findings -- catching vulnerabilities before deploy (shift-left).

clues.clue: This HashiCorp tool defines cloud infrastructure using declarative configuration files in HCL and tracks state to plan incremental changes.
clues.explain: Terraform declares infrastructure in HCL and tracks state, generating a plan of incremental changes to reach the desired config across many cloud providers.

clues.clue: This Ansible concept is a YAML file that defines an ordered set of tasks to execute on a group of managed hosts.
clues.explain: An Ansible playbook is a YAML list of ordered tasks run against host groups -- agentless, over SSH, to configure systems.

clues.clue: This IaC principle guarantees that running the same configuration multiple times always produces the same result, preventing duplicate resources.
clues.explain: Idempotency means re-running the same config yields the same end state without duplicating resources -- core to safe, repeatable automation.

clues.clue: This Terraform file records the real-world status of every managed resource and is compared against the desired configuration to compute a plan.
clues.explain: terraform.tfstate records the real resources Terraform manages and is diffed against your config to compute the plan; it must be protected and locked.

clues.clue: This operational model treats infrastructure definitions as application code, storing them in version control with pull request reviews and automated CI tests before applying.
clues.response: What is GitOps (or Infrastructure as Code with CI/CD)?
clues.explain: GitOps treats Git as the single source of truth for infrastructure: changes go through PRs and CI, and an agent reconciles the live system to match the repo.
